\caption[The cost of one forward evaluation, and what it amortises to]{The cost of one forward evaluation, and what it amortises to. Medians over the timed draws, each the minimum of at least seven repetitions, on one core. The two error columns are the metric of Table~\ref{tab:metrics} on the elements of $\mathbf{U}$: the worst off-diagonal element that exists where the system is coupled, the elastic element where it is not. They are read off $2000$ validation draws, none of them seen in training; the p95 in particular needs a sample of that size to be an estimate rather than close to the largest value observed. Absolute times reproduce to between $5$ and $30$ per cent between runs, so the gain against the $V$-only baseline is \emph{paired}, baseline and prediction timed on the same $\theta$ microseconds apart; the other two are unpaired and rounded. It is a median of per-draw ratios, so it does not equal the ratio of the two median columns. \textbf{The R-matrix column is an upper bound, not the cost of the method}: that implementation rebuilds a $\theta$-independent kinetic matrix on every call and inverts where $N_c$ right-hand sides would do. The gain against $V$ only is the one to defend. Each configuration is the cheapest the autocalibration proposes that clears the posterior tolerance. Two things this table is not. The offline cost is paid \emph{per energy node and per $J^\pi$ block}: a campaign over twenty energies pays it twenty times, so the training minutes quoted here are not the training cost of a full campaign. And every time in it is Python against Python. It is the ratio that carries over to another implementation, not the absolute values: a compiled solver would move both the baseline and the emulator columns.}
